pillar: Thyroid Cancer Treatment in India for International Patients

items.q: How much does thyroid cancer treatment cost in India?
items.a: Thyroid cancer treatment in India usually costs between USD 4,000 and USD 8,000 for a total thyroidectomy, and radioactive iodine therapy adds about USD 1,500 to USD 3,000. The final figure depends on the hospital, the city, the stage of your disease, and whether neck lymph node dissection is needed. Costs may change once your reports are reviewed, so ask for a written estimate before you travel.

items.q: Is thyroid cancer curable if I come to India for treatment?
items.a: Most thyroid cancers are highly treatable, and papillary and follicular types have 10-year survival rates above 90 percent when caught early. Treatment in India follows the same protocols used in Europe and the United States: surgery, radioactive iodine, and thyroid hormone suppression. Outcomes depend on your cancer type, stage, and age rather than on where you are treated, so ask your oncologist what your specific reports suggest.

items.q: How long will I need to stay in India for thyroid cancer treatment?
items.a: Plan for three to four weeks in India if you need surgery followed by radioactive iodine. Thyroidectomy involves two to three days in hospital and about ten days of recovery before travel clearance. Radioactive iodine requires a short isolation stay and a scan a few days later. Your total stay may be longer if lymph node surgery, a second iodine dose, or extra scans are needed.

items.q: Do I need radioactive iodine after thyroid surgery?
items.a: Not everyone does. Radioactive iodine is usually recommended for larger tumours, cancer that has spread to lymph nodes or beyond the thyroid, or aggressive tumour subtypes. Small, low-risk papillary cancers under one centimetre are often treated with surgery alone. Your team decides using the pathology report, thyroglobulin levels, and post-surgery scans, so the decision is usually made a few weeks after the operation rather than before you travel.

items.q: Which hospitals in India treat thyroid cancer for international patients?
items.a: India's major cancer centres in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad all run dedicated head and neck or endocrine surgery units with nuclear medicine departments on site. Look for a hospital with a high-volume thyroid surgeon, an in-house radioactive iodine isolation ward, and NABH or JCI accreditation. CancerFax can help you compare centres and share your reports with them, though your treating oncology team makes the final plan.

items.q: Will I have a visible scar on my neck after thyroid surgery?
items.a: Yes, most thyroid operations leave a horizontal scar low on the neck, usually four to eight centimetres long, which fades considerably over six to twelve months. Many Indian centres also offer scarless approaches such as transoral or robotic thyroidectomy, where the incision is hidden inside the lip or under the armpit. Whether you qualify depends on tumour size and whether lymph nodes are involved, so ask your surgeon during the first consultation.

items.q: What is a medical visa for India and how do I get one?
items.a: An Indian medical visa, or e-Medical visa, is granted on the basis of a treatment invitation letter from a recognised Indian hospital. You apply online with your passport, a photograph, your medical reports, and the hospital letter, and approval often takes three to five working days. Two attendants can travel with you on medical attendant visas. Processing times and eligibility depend on your nationality and current rules.

items.q: Do I have to take thyroid medication for life after treatment?
items.a: Yes, if your whole thyroid is removed you will take levothyroxine tablets every day for life. The dose is not just replacement; after cancer it is often set slightly higher to suppress the hormone that can stimulate remaining thyroid cells. You need a blood test every six to twelve weeks at first, then less often. The tablets are inexpensive and available in most countries, so follow-up can usually continue at home.

items.q: How is medullary or anaplastic thyroid cancer treated differently in India?
items.a: Medullary and anaplastic thyroid cancers do not respond to radioactive iodine, so treatment relies on surgery, radiotherapy, and targeted drugs instead. Indian centres use targeted therapies such as vandetanib, cabozantinib, and selpercatinib for medullary disease, and genetic testing for RET mutations guides the choice. Anaplastic cancer is aggressive and often needs radiation with chemotherapy started quickly. Access to newer drugs and trials may vary by hospital.

items.q: What reports should I send before travelling for thyroid cancer treatment?
items.a: Send your neck ultrasound, the fine needle aspiration or biopsy report, thyroid function tests, and any CT or PET scan images on a disc or shared link. If you have already had surgery, add the operative note and histopathology report. CancerFax can pass these to Indian centres for a written opinion and estimate before you book flights. A hospital may still repeat some tests after you arrive.
